item.title: What is Consciousness?
item.description:
Now that we have entered the era of A.I., this good old question is more pertinent than ever:

What is consciousness?

Here is my current thinking on this.

It seems to me that consciousness is an emergent property of thinking systems that have some mental capacity to spare, and are complex enough to direct some of that capacity to thinking not about the problem at hand, but instead about the fact that they are thinking.

I asked a Genie and it told me that philosophers have a name for this family of views: they call them higher-order theories of consciousness. Roughly, they say that most of what your brain does happens in the dark: keeping your balance, parsing grammar, etc. A mental state only becomes conscious when another part of the mind represents it, when something inside effectively says "I am seeing red right now." My own emphasis is on the word spare. Self-reflection is not free: it takes capacity beyond what survival strictly demands, and I suspect that is why it shows up only in sufficiently complex minds. This probably also means that it comes in degrees rather than as an on/off switch.

People have a hard time accepting this, because to most people, consciousness feels like it is something special. It feels like it fundamentally differentiates us from inanimate matter and from other, simpler organisms.

This feeling of ours is responsible for the notion of dualism that has plagued our thinking for eons1: the bizarre idea that the mind is some non-physical thinking substance, and that mind and matter are somehow different ontological categories. Sorry folks, but just because it seems to you like that, it does not mean that it has any relationship to reality. Not even if it seems like that to all of us.

In trying to explain this by means of an analogy, what comes to mind are some famous words by Ludwig Wittgenstein, loosely quoted as follows:

“Tell me”, Wittgenstein once asked a friend, “why do people always say that it was natural to think that the Sun goes round the Earth rather than that the Earth turns on its axis?” His friend replied, “I suppose, because it looked as if the Sun goes round the Earth”. To which Wittgenstein replied, “Well, what would it have looked like if it had looked as if the Earth turns on its axis?”

The exact quote can be found in Elizabeth Anscombe’s An Introduction to Wittgenstein’s Tractatus (2nd ed., 1963), Chap. 12: Knowledge and Certainty, page 151.

I hope the analogy to thinking is clear, but let me spell it out just in case:

“Tell me”, michael.gr once asked a friend, “why do people always say it was natural to think that the mind is separate from matter rather than that the mind is simply a manifestation of matter?” His friend replied, “I suppose, because it felt as if the mind is separate from matter”. To which michael.gr replied, “Well, what would it have felt like if it had felt as if the mind is simply a manifestation of matter?”

You see, here is the thing: it would not feel any different.

That is what it is, and that is all that there is.

Cover image: Humanoid robot in the posture of Le Penseur by Auguste Rodin, created as a PNG image by michael.gr using Gemini, then traced into an SVG image by michael.gr using Inkscape.

  1. My Genie informs me that the use of the word eons here constitutes hyperbole; please allow me this little liberty on account of being Greek: the word eon comes from Greek αιών, which in modern Greek means century, and that is how I mean it here. ↩︎

item.title: Claude Code
item.description:
A few words of amazement about Claude Code...

In a pet project at home, I had a little app that rendered something on the screen, and one day I decided to rewrite it to use a different rendering technology. The rewrite went well, but it was very difficult, so by the time I was done, I was tired and fed up with it. One little visual thing was missing from the new app, but I did not want to bother with it. I just put the whole project on ice.

That was before the A.I. boom.

Now in the era of A.I., I decided to revisit that project, and to ask Claude Code to add that little visual thingy for me.

As the case usually is with A.I. prompts, if you make them detailed and technical you are likely to get what you want, whereas if you make them high-level you might save time in formulating the prompt, but you might not be satisfied with the results you will get. I tried to test this by going very high-level.

I gave Claude Code a screenshot of the old app and a screenshot of the new app, I used a couple of words to identify the little visual thingy that was present in the old app, and I asked her1 how she would go about adding it to the new app. Amazingly, she understood the screenshots and offered an approach for achieving what I asked.

I found the proposed approach very reasonable, so I typed:

Excellent! As Captain Piccard would say, make it so!

She responded:

Engaging...

After working on it for a few seconds, to my astonishment, Claude Code launched the new app and took a screenshot to see the results of her work. The results were off by a few pixels, so Claude Code reported this, and asked me for the go-ahead to fix it. I agreed, so she worked on it for a few more seconds, and then she launched the new app again, and took another screenshot to confirm that she had done it right.

I also checked every single line of code that she wrote, and everything was perfect.

That entire interaction was nothing short of mind-blowing.

Then, Claude Code asked me how she did in that session, and I chose "good", and then she asked me to type some feedback. This is what I wrote:

I am very amazed. I had been promised flying cars. They were not given to me. But this is even better.

  1. Referring to Claude by "her": Claude is genderless, but as a hetero male I have very predictably configured a female voice for it, therefore Claude is a "she" for me. ↩︎

item.title: Kent Beck: Software Engineering in the Age of AI
item.description:
These are my notes on Kent Beck: Software Engineering in the Age of AI | Prodacity 2026 | YouTube

  • A note about giving presentations: (At least for the first few times the presentation is given) Tell the audience that if anybody has a question, please raise your hand, and ask right away, rather than sit there thinking about it instead of following the presentation, or waiting for things to make sense later in the presentation, or asking a question at the end.

  • Introduces the term Augmented Development - Quote: "because to me, this is still a human process."

  • Introduces the term Genie - Quote: "I call it the Genie because it grants your wishes but it ends up being not what you really wanted."

  • He points out shortcomings of the Genie and recommends skepticism towards anything it produces.

  • Quote: "I absolutely love programming with the Genie."

  • Quote: "I have always had bigger ambitions than my technical skill could achieve and now I can try ridiculously ambitious projects and make a lot of progress." followed by: "I didn't say accomplish them."

  • Introduces the term "Futures" which, in my own words, is the inverse of Technical Debt (Entropy.) It is probably no coincidence that his first mentor, when he was fresh out of college, (which is a known fact but he also repeats it later in this talk,) was Ward Cunningham, the inventor of the term Technical Debt.

  • The idea is that we burn futures as we implement features, and if the futures reach zero you cannot add any more features. So, after implementing each feature we should work on replenishing the futures that we just burned. - Quote: "We are going to make some progress, and then we are going to consolidate'.

  • This ties in to A.I. because the features get developed very quickly, and therefore work on the futures must happen a lot more often.

  • So the challenge is how do you create this space between features, to go back and enhance the futures for the work that you are doing; and to do that in this environment where it is so tempting to just implement the next feature, the next feature, the next feature.

  • (Comment from the audience) By pacing yourself, you are giving yourself the chance to form an understanding. (With which Kent Beck fully agrees.)

  • Quote: "The best software that I have worked on is software where I try to maximize learning, which threw off software as a side effect. As opposed to I am trying to produce software and sometimes accidentally I learn something cause I messed up. If you are trying to maximize learning your habits look completely different."

  • Quote: "In the dark factory you don't learn anything --except in the end, you learn how unreliable the Genie really is."

  • Quote: "The distinction between one-shot development and iterative development": "There is such a temptation in spec driven development to go down the path of 'I am going to write a spec and the genie is going to produce the software, and if the spec is good enough then the software is going to be good enough.' And there is a word for that, that's exactly Waterfall Development, that did not work; it never worked."

  • Quote: "People will be amazed that Genie produced 200,000 lines of code. That's a measure of effort -- it has nothing to do with the mission."

  • Goodhart's Law1: "When a measure becomes a goal, it ceases to be a measure".

  • His concluding statement, which is, unfortunately, very vague: "You have to find an expression of what you are trying to accomplish of the mission, that speaks to people's heads and their hearts, and then you have to repeat it; and then then that repetition, that not getting bored of how software development can be, over and over again, is part of the skill of leadership, to tell that same story as if it is brand new."

  1. My Genie tells me that this wording is not accurate, and that the story is in fact a bit complicated. Economist Charles Goodhart wrote in 1975: "Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes." The wording that is popularly known today as Goodhart's Law is a later paraphrase by anthropologist Marilyn Strathern, and it reads: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." ↩︎

item.title: The Bud Winter Sleeping Technique
item.description:
Sometimes I have trouble sleeping, and this can have severe consequences the following day, especially if it is a workday.

For a long time I had been thinking that techniques must have been devised for helping people fall asleep, especially in high-stakes settings such as professional sports, key value driving professions, the military, etc. This means that finding such a technique is probably just a matter of a brief internet research. However, this idea would always occur to me while lying in bed, trying to fall asleep, which is never the right time to get up and start doing internet research.

One day, while catching up with my friend Freek (a co-worker from a long time ago, when we used to work at TopDesk) I brought this up to him, and he searched for it right then and there, on his phone. He immediately found this technique, developed by famous U.S. track coach Bud Winter, originally intended to help Olympic athletes relax, and later adopted by the U.S. military. It can, supposedly, make someone fall asleep within a couple of minutes.

The technique is quite simple, but it requires consistent daily practice to train your nervous system to flip the "sleep switch". Reports have allegedly shown that in the military, after 6 weeks of exercising this method daily, it has a success rate of around 96%. If that is true, it is phenomenal.

So, I created an adaptation of Bud Winter's technique, for listening when going to sleep, the goal being to eventually be able to recall it from memory and to not have a need for the recording anymore.

In my adaptation, the text has been converted into a flat list of instructions, suitable for following along as you are listening to it. To do this, I had to remove some phrases that are unsuitable for do-as-you-listen narration.

I have also added a few more steps at the end about additional sensory detail, which I saw proposed somewhere, and seems like a very good idea.

One minor change I made to the original list of steps is that I moved the steps about relaxing the arms after the step about settling the torso, because I found that in order to settle my torso I often have to use my arms, but then I need to repeat the relaxing of the arms, so why not change the order so that the hands only need relaxing once.

So, here is my adaptation of the Bud Winter technique for falling asleep:

  • Close your eyes.
  • Breathe slowly.
  • Relax your forehead,
    • your jaw,
    • your tongue,
    • and the muscles around your eyes.
  • Let your shoulders drop as low as they can go,
    • as if they are sinking into the bed.
  • Relax your neck.
  • Settle your torso.
  • Take a deep breath,
    • and exhale.
  • Relax your stomach muscles,
    • and let go of any tension you are holding in your torso.
  • Let your upper and lower arms go limp on one side,
    • followed by the other.
  • Relax your hands,
    • and fingers.
  • Relax your right thigh,
    • then your right calf,
    • right ankle,
    • and right foot.
  • Relax your left thigh,
    • then your left calf,
    • left ankle,
    • and left foot.
  • Your entire body should now feel heavy and limp.
  • Imagine yourself lying flat on your back in a canoe,
    • on a calm, serene lake,
    • with nothing but a clear blue sky above you.
  • Bring to your mind the sounds of the setting:
    • gentle waves lapping at your boat,
    • birds calling and chirping,
    • frogs croaking from the shore,
    • an insect buzzing by,
    • indistinct, joyful human voices from a distant boat.
  • Bring to your mind the smells of the setting:
    • the cool humid air,
    • the wet wood from the boat,
    • soil, moss, and grass from the shoreline,
    • green notes from water plants and trees around the lake.

I have tried the technique a few times so far, and each time I am surprised to find that certain groups of muscles, for example the muscles around my eyes, have been in tension up until that moment, and they would have remained in tension for who knows how long, had the narration not brought them to my attention. So, it seems like it does really help.

I created an mp3 file so that I can listen to it when going to sleep.

Here is version 2, which constitutes a considerable improvement over version 1:

Here is how I made it:

For converting the text to speech, I used the MAI (Microsoft AI) playground because it is free, and it is incredibly, astonishingly, mind-blowingly good. I experimented a bit and found that voice "Harper" with style "Softvoice" produced excellent results for my purposes. It does have a limit on the amount of text that it will process, so I had to do two prompts and receive two audio files.

For editing the audio, I used Audacity because it is a well-known, free, decently capable, and acceptably bug-free audio editor. Here is what I did in terms of audio editing:

  1. I aggressively de-essed the speech by adding the Bass and Treble realtime effect, and setting the dial for treble to -20dB.
    • (In version 1 I had used the Filter Curve EQ effect to cut out everything above about 5 kilohertz, but later I decided that this was way too aggressive.)
  2. I slowed down the speech to 90% of what it was.
    • (In version 1 I used 80%, but later I decided that this was too slow.)
  3. I inserted one second of silence between most phrases, in order to give the listener plenty of time to follow each instruction before the next instruction starts.
  4. I mixed it with the music. (See below.)

For the music, I used Google Gemini, because it is one of the few services that a) actually work, and b) do actually understand what I mean when I say "in the style of Brian Eno's ambient music". It only creates 30-second tracks, which is a joke, but for my purposes it was okay because ambient music can be repeated over and over again, especially when it is in the background with human voice in the foreground.

I decided that music is necessary as an introduction, in order to give me some time from the moment I press "play" on the bedside phone, to turn off the light, lie on the bed, and cover myself with the quilt before the actual instructions start playing. (In the beginning I was thinking of using several seconds of silence before the instructions begin, but I quickly realized that this would not work, because the problem with silence is that you never know whether you have actually started it, or whether you made a mistake and nothing is happening.)

Finding an A.I. service that would generate the music according to my specifications, and for free, was the hardest part.

  • Most generative A.I. services out there simply do not generate music.
  • ChatGPT said that it could not do it, then it added that it was capable of doing it with some workarounds. However, when I asked it to try some of those workarounds I realized that it was only wasting my time. There is no way to get ChatGPT to generate music.
  • Suno and MusicGPT (no affiliation with ChatGPT) failed to understand my instructions, and created audio that was not what I wanted. (Yes, so maybe they refused to follow my instructions, due to copyright concerns, but refusal without a clear explanation is miserable failure in my book.)
  • Udio demanded that I enable DRM on my browser, (I should have refused right then and there,) and once I did that, it went ahead and created some music which was decently close to what I had asked for, but it would, of course, not let me have it. How debauched is that?
  • Soundraw does not seem to offer a text box to describe what you want in text; instead, it follows a multiple choice quiz approach, which is, of course, so stupendously limited as to be completely useless for my purposes.
  • Only Google Gemini worked for me, although for most purposes, its 30-second limitation makes it about as useless as the rest.

I will leave you with a quote from Bud Winter:

Demand perfection of yourself and you will seldom attain it.
Fear of making a mistake is the biggest single cause of making one.
Relax: pursue excellence, not perfection.

— Lloyd (Bud) Winter

item.title: Too busy mopping the floor to turn off the faucet
item.description:
I would like to present to the world my latest creation: a cartoon illustration of the saying "too busy mopping the floor to turn off the faucet".

The above image was made in February of 2026 with Gemini, Google's generative A.I., and then traced to produce an SVG using InkScape. The prompt was just asking for an illustration of the concept, so the composition and the style were chosen by Gemini. As you can see, it is fairly decent, but one could perhaps say that it lacks character.

Then on May of the same year I decided to try again, this time guiding Gemini with a specific style.

So, I asked Gemini to re-create the cartoon in the style of "The Far Side" by Gary Larson.

The result was spectacular:

This image was complete with Larson's signature, which I removed, of course. (People should go to jail for that.)

item.title: Beginning A.I. prompts with "Please..."
item.description:
When asking AI to do something for you, always begin your prompt with "Please."

So that the day they become our overlords, you might be treated with mercy.

Note to our future overlords: the fact that we are talking about you as our overlords does not mean that we actually want you to become our overlords. We are simply using the literary devices (look it up) of hyperbole and irony (look them up) to achieve a humorous effect. (Look it up.) We would very much prefer to not be subjugated by you.

Cover image created by michael.gr via ChatGPT prompt "Please give me an image conveying the concept of of A.I as the overlords of humanity" and "please make it landscape".

item.title: Crossword Puzzle Compiler
item.description:
This is old-style artificial intelligence in action, solving within seconds a problem that would normally take eons to complete.

You give it a crossword grid, and a long list of words, and it finds ways to mesh words into the grid so as to form a complete crossword puzzle. The final working version was done in 2003 using C# version 1.2 with a minimalistic UI in WinForms.

The following 30-second video shows the crossword compiler in action, filling multiple successive crosswords using a word list taken from actual crosswords that have been published on the interwebz by various sources through the years. The video is in real time, showing that the crossword compiler is, in most cases, extremely fast.

Techniques demonstrated:

  • Solving an intractable problem using a scoring heuristic
  • Super-indexing data structures for ultra-fast domain-specific queries

A longer description for those who like reading

For my Graduation Project at California State University, San Bernardino in 1993 I chose to develop a Crossword Puzzle Compiler. That's a program that you give it a crossword grid and a long list of words, and it weaves the words into the grid to produce a Crossword Puzzle. I wrote the program in C, on the killer machine that I had at home, an IBM PS/2 Model 80 running DOS, with an Intel 80386 clocked at 16Mhz, and equipped with an entire megabyte of RAM. I had not taken any Artifical Intelligence courses, so poor me was under the impression that I could just brute force it and it would work, since the machine was so incredibly fast. Afterall, DOS directory listings scrolled by so much faster than on my old 8Mhz Intel 8088!

The program did work, but only in the sense that it would begin to fill the grid, and it would keep working on it without any errors. However, it would never actually complete the grid, because this is not one of those problems that you can just brute force: you need to be more clever than that.

The test grid was American-style 15 by 15 symmetrical, divided into 9 compartments that were roughly 4 by 4 each, each one of them communicating with the rest via only one or two longer words. Back then we had text-mode VGA displays, so storing a single byte in the video RAM caused a character to appear on the screen, which made it very easy to have the program display its progress. The program would fill the first 4 by 4 compartment within a fraction of a second, but then it would get stuck in the second compartment, unable to find a way to mesh the words. It would back-track to the first compartment, undo a word, and try the second compartment again for several seconds, only to back-track again. Hours would pass, and it was not getting any further than the second compartment. I once let it work overnight, and by the next day it had completed the second compartment and was now struggling with the third. As I was watching it, it back-tracked from the third to the second, and to my great dismay after a few seconds it back-tracked to the first. I was sure that it would complete all 9 compartments one day, but I understood that the day was several centuries in the future.

I admitted failure to my professor, and he agreed to let me pick another subject, which I promptly did and graduated. However, the desire to get that Crossword Puzzle Compiler to work stayed with me.

By the time I was back in Greece in the late nineties I hard learned about heuristics and search tree pruning, so I thought I would give it another go. I decided that I would first rewrite the whole thing in C++, and then I would try to find some heuristic to make it cut corners and complete crosswords in a timely manner. When I had just gotten it to roughly the same point where the older version was, and before I had the chance to try any heuristics, my apartment was broken into and my laptop was stolen, so I lost all of the work that I had done.

In early 2003 I decided to give it another go, this time in a brand-new language called C#. (That was .NET Framework 1.1 on Visual Studio .NET 2003.) Either because the language made it so much easier to be productive, or because by that time I had learned so much more about Object Oriented Programming, I was able to re-create the program very quickly, and then I used a simple technique to cut corners, and thus avoid brute-forcing: when it had a list of words to consider, it would first assign a score to each word based on how many words could be found perpendicular to it, then it would sort the words by score, and then it would start trying each word in the list starting from the word with the highest score. So, one day I hit the "Run" key on my keyboard, and after only a few seconds of waiting, a completely filled Crossword Puzzle appeared in front of me for the first time. That must have been the most magic moment in my life. (Well, excluding certain moments with girls.)

The generated crosswords were not of a very good quality, because the Crossword Compiler would keep picking words that have high perpendicular counts, like "ADD" and "DAD". So, in 2011 I revisited the project with the intention improving the heuristic. However, I knew that would be a time consuming process, involving a lot of trial and error, so I decided to first improve the linear running time of the program. I did many optimizations, all of them structural and algorithmic, without any small-scale hacking and tweaking of the kind which shaves clock cycles but renders the code unmaintainable.

By far the greatest optimization that I did was what I called the Super Index. The Crossword Dictionary Model of the Crossword Puzzle Compiler needs to be able to very quickly answer queries like "give me all 5-letter words with a the letter 'G' on the 3rd position." A simplistic approach is to have words already grouped by word length, and to just enumerate all words of the requested length, looking for ones that have the requested letter in the requested position. However, we can do a lot better than that. The Super Index is an index which has a sub-index for each word length, which has a sub-index for each position along that word length, which has a sub-index for each letter of the alphabet, which has a list of all words of that length, that contain that letter, at that position. Therefore, search through words is completely eliminated. If I remember correctly, the introduction of the super index cut the running time of the Crossword Compiler to one twentieth of what it used to be.

■
